strengths: Addresses a highly practical and relevant task: high-resolution image editing (e.g., 2K resolution) without requiring model retraining or massive GPU memory.
Proposes a novel and lightweight 1x1 convolution as a learnable feature-space transfer function, which effectively transfers high-frequency details while maintaining spatial structures.

Introduces a clever non-overlapping patch synchronization mechanism (using blended-Tweedie updates and a resampling strategy) that avoids the high computational overhead of traditional overlapping patch sampling.

Demonstrates strong performance across multiple metrics (HaarPSI, masked PSNR/SSIM) against competitive baselines consisting of state-of-the-art low-resolution editing followed by advanced diffusion-based super-resolution.
Shows good generalization capability, showing compatibility with both UNet-based (Stable Diffusion 2.1) and Transformer-based (FLUX.1-dev) architectures.
weaknesses: Lack of runtime/complexity analysis: Since the method relies on test-time optimization of the transfer function for each image, it likely incurs a non-trivial computational overhead. The paper should provide a detailed comparison of inference/optimization latency against the baselines.

Limited comparison to other high-resolution diffusion baselines: While comparing to 'LR-editing + SR' is logical, the paper would be stronger if it also compared against or discussed other training-free high-resolution generation/editing paradigms (e.g., adapting DemoFusion [10] or FreeScale [35] directly for the editing task).

Heavy dependence on the quality of the low-resolution reference edit: Any geometric distortion or semantic failure from the initial low-resolution editor (e.g., NanoBanana) is propagated and amplified in the high-resolution output.

The details of the evaluation dataset (comprising 400 cases generated via ChatGPT and FreeScale) are sparse, and it is unclear if the dataset and the benchmark code will be publicly released to facilitate reproducibility.

strengths: Introduces a practical and effective test-time optimization framework (ScaleEdit) for high-resolution image editing (>1K/2K) using existing pretrained low-resolution diffusion models.

The proposed feature-space transfer function (a lightweight learnable $1\times1$ convolution) effectively transfers micro-scale details from the high-resolution source to the target image in a spatially adaptive manner.

The patch synchronization mechanism, utilizing blended Tweedie predictions and a resampling strategy, successfully alleviates boundary artifacts and ensures global consistency without requiring costly overlapping patch inference.
Demonstrates strong generalization across different model architectures, showing compatibility with both Stable Diffusion (UNet-based) and FLUX (Transformer-based) backbones.
Provides solid quantitative and qualitative improvements over baseline workflows that combine low-resolution editing with state-of-the-art super-resolution methods.
weaknesses: Lack of discussion on computational overhead and inference/optimization time. Since the method optimizes a $1\times1$ convolution layer per patch over multiple diffusion timesteps, the test-time optimization cost could be significant (especially for 2K/4K images with many patches). Quantitative reporting of the time taken per image is highly desirable.

The dependence on the quality of the low-resolution editing model (e.g., NanoBanana) is a notable limitation. If the low-resolution edit introduces artifacts or fails to capture the text prompt, these issues will directly propagate to the high-resolution output.

Analysis of the alignment under significant structural or semantic changes (e.g., object replacement where shapes differ drastically) could be strengthened, as the $1\times1$ convolution primarily preserves spatial layouts.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and challenging task: high-resolution image editing (2K and above) without requiring resource-heavy training of a new high-resolution diffusion model.
The proposed detail enhancement module using a learnable 1x1 convolution effectively maps low-resolution feature trajectories to high-resolution ones, preserving fine-grained micro-textures.

The synchronization strategy (incorporating blended Tweedie updates and a resampling strategy) solves the boundary artifact problem of non-overlapping patch-wise inference in an elegant manner without requiring expensive overlapping window sampling.

Strong quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate clear superiority over standard cascade pipelines (editing followed by super-resolution) and show applicability to both Stable Diffusion and FLUX backbones.
weaknesses: The test-time optimization nature of ScaleEdit, which requires optimizing a 1x1 convolution parameter for each patch and across multiple timesteps, is likely computationally heavy. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of inference time and GPU memory usage (e.g., comparing it with the cascade baselines or other patch-based methods).
There is a minor inconsistency in the hyperparameter τ description: Section 5.1 mentions τ=15 is used as default, whereas the ablation study in Section D / Table 2 states the default setting is τ=35.

The comparison only includes Cascade baselines (editing + Super Resolution). A comparison or discussion with training-free high-resolution generation/editing methods like DemoFusion or ScaleCrafter adapted for image editing would make the evaluation more comprehensive.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and challenging task: high-resolution image editing using standard, fixed-resolution pretrained models.
The proposed method (ScaleEdit) uses a clever test-time optimization of a lightweight 1x1 convolution feature transfer function to preserve high-resolution details from the source image.
The patch synchronization mechanism (Blended Tweedie with a resampling strategy) is technically sound and avoids the heavy computational overhead of traditional overlapping patch methods.
The method demonstrates good generalizability, working with both U-Net (Stable Diffusion) and Transformer-based (FLUX.1-dev) architectures.
Strong qualitative and quantitative results outperforming several diffusion-based super-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world image datasets.
weaknesses: The computational overhead is quite high due to the test-time optimization. As shown in the supplementary materials, the runtime is 234.77 seconds (without NTI) and 635.51 seconds (with NTI) per image on an NVIDIA A6000, which limits its applicability to real-world interactive or real-time workflows.

The framework acts as a guided detail-transfer/upscaling tool rather than an independent end-to-end editor, heavily relying on a pre-existing low-resolution edited reference image. Artifacts or semantic errors in the low-resolution editing step will propagate directly to the final high-resolution output.

The choice of hyperparameter tau (the step at which optimization begins) requires manual empirical tuning depending on the desired balance between source structure preservation and style/edit strength.

strengths: Innovative Task Formulation: The paper presents an elegant framework to address high-resolution image editing by leveraging low-resolution edited reference images and high-resolution source details, bypassing the resolution limitations of pretrained diffusion models.

Strong Technical Contribution: The introduction of a spatially adaptive 1x1 convolution as a learnable feature-level transfer function is novel. Additionally, the non-overlapping patch synchronization scheme, combining blended Tweedie updates with a resampling strategy, successfully avoids the computational overhead of overlapping patch inference while mitigating grid artifacts.

Robust Architecture Generalization: The method is shown to be highly generalizable, working effectively across different backbones, including U-Net based architectures (Stable Diffusion 2.1) and Diffusion Transformers (FLUX.1-dev).

Detailed Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation: ScaleEdit shows clear superior performance over 'edit-then-super-resolve' baselines in preserving high-resolution structures and textures, supported by comprehensive ablation studies.
weaknesses: Significant Computational Overhead: Due to the test-time optimization of the transfer function (and optional Null-text inversion), the runtime is high, taking between 234 and 635 seconds per image on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU. This severely limits its practicality for interactive editing workflows.

Limited Scope of Baselines: The baseline comparison is restricted to low-res editing followed by super-resolution. The evaluation would be stronger if compared against training-free high-resolution generation/editing techniques (e.g., DemoFusion, ScaleCrafter, or MultiDiffusion/tiling) adapted to editing.

Heavy Dependency on Low-Resolution References: Since the pipeline requires an external low-resolution edited image as a reference, any semantic errors, structural distortions, or editing failures introduced by the low-resolution editing model will propagate and affect the final high-resolution output.

Lack of Human Evaluation: Image editing quality is highly subjective. A user study measuring semantic alignment and perceptual detail preservation would provide stronger empirical evidence than automated metrics alone.

strengths: Effective High-Resolution Editing: The paper presents ScaleEdit, a practical and effective framework that successfully edits high-resolution images (2K, 8K) using existing generative models trained on low resolutions (e.g., SD, FLUX), preserving fine-grained micro-textures.

Generative Prior Transfer via Learnable $1 \times 1$ Conv: The use of a lightweight, spatially-adaptive transfer function (modeled as a $1 \times 1$ convolution) optimized at test-time is technically sound and elegantly aligns low-resolution structures with high-resolution details.

Training-Free & Cross-Architecture Generalization: The method is training-free and demonstrates robust generalization across both U-Net (Stable Diffusion) and Transformer-based (FLUX.1-dev) architectures.

Novel Synchronization Strategy: The proposed non-overlapping patch synchronization scheme, combining blended Tweedie updates with a resampling strategy, effectively eliminates boundary artifacts without the heavy computational overhead of overlapping patch inference.

Thorough Evaluation: The paper provides solid quantitative comparisons (using metrics like HaarPSI, LPIPS, M-MSE) and compelling qualitative results, along with detailed ablation studies in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: High Computational Complexity: The test-time optimization of the transfer function per patch, combined with the optional Null-Text Inversion and the resampling step (which requires an extra forward step per denoising step), results in a very high execution time. According to Appendix G, the process takes over 234 seconds (without NTI) and up to 635 seconds (with NTI) for 1K editing on an NVIDIA A6000, which limits interactive or real-time editing use cases.

Heavy Dependence on Low-Resolution References: The method acts as a detail-transfer model conditioned on a low-resolution edited image. Thus, the editing quality is strictly bounded by the capability of the low-resolution editor. Any semantic errors or artifacts in the low-resolution reference will propagate to the final high-resolution output.

Clarity on Computational Overhead Comparison: While the paper notes that the synchronization avoids overlapping inference to decrease cost, a direct runtime/memory comparison against standard overlapping patch methods (like those used in MultiDiffusion or DemoFusion) would better justify the added complexity of the resampling strategy.

Overstated Novelty Claims: The authors claim to be the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task. While this specific patch-wise detail-transfer setting is unique, editing high-resolution images has been previously explored in various contexts (e.g., via high-resolution generation with control nets or inpainting, or local editing with super-resolution). This claim should be better contextualized.
